## Agenda {.agenda}

1. Use the command line to describe actions precisely
2. Use Git to record useful versions of a research project
3. Use branches to separate exploratory work
4. Make one version reproducible by another person

::: {.notes}
The lecture has two connected layers. Git records project history. Reproducible
research requires enough information to run a selected version again.

The command line is supporting material. Teach only the concepts needed to
understand the Git examples and scripted research workflows.

Suggested timing: motivation and command line, 15 minutes; Git's data model,
20 minutes; individual workflow, 25 minutes; reproducibility, 15 minutes;
summary and questions, 5 minutes.
:::

## The goal

At the end of the semester, you should be able to answer:

1. What changed?
2. Why did it change?
3. Which version produced this result?
4. Can another person produce it again?

::: {.notes}
These questions apply to your future self, an adviser, a research assistant,
or an AI agent. Version control answers the first three questions. The complete
research workflow answers the fourth question.
:::

## Organization without version control

```text
analysis.py
analysis_new.py
analysis_final.py
analysis_final_fixed.py
analysis_final_final_no_seriously.py
```

**Prediction:** Which file produced the table in the paper?

::: {.notes}
Pause before asking for answers. The filenames record guesses about importance,
not a reliable history. Copies also hide which lines changed and why.

The problem is not only untidy filenames. The researcher cannot connect a
result to a precise state of the complete project.
:::

## Version control records project states

```text
●  Estimate baseline model
│
●  Correct treatment coding
│
●  Import raw survey data
```

Each **commit** records a project snapshot and an explanation.

::: {.notes}
Define a commit as a recorded project snapshot plus metadata. The metadata
include its parent, author, time, and message.

Git usually stores file differences efficiently, but the useful mental model
is a sequence or graph of complete project states.
:::

## Version control changes how you work

| Without Git | With Git |
|---|---|
| Copy files to preserve versions | Record a commit |
| Recall last month's changes | Inspect the history |
| Fear an unsuccessful experiment | Create a branch |
| Lose the last working version | Return to a prior commit |

::: {.notes}
For independent research, Git is primarily an organization and recovery tool.
Collaboration is an important extension, but it is not the organizing case for
this course.
:::

## A reproducible result

> Another person can use the same inputs and instructions to produce the same result.

Git preserves the version. Git does not preserve the complete computing environment.

::: {.notes}
Distinguish version control from reproducibility now. A repository can preserve
the exact analysis code while omitting the data, package versions, seed, or run
instructions. That repository has useful history but may not be reproducible.
:::

## Command line interface {.section-divider}

## Three parts of a command-line session

<div class="three-part">
<div><strong>Terminal</strong><br><span>Displays text</span></div>
<div><strong>Shell</strong><br><span>Interprets commands</span></div>
<div><strong>Program</strong><br><span>Performs an action</span></div>
</div>

```text
$ git status
```

::: {.notes}
The terminal is the window. The shell reads the command. Git is the program
that the shell starts. Students do not need the implementation details, but
these terms prevent later confusion.

The shell is valuable because each action has a textual representation. The
same command can be inspected, repeated, documented, and given to an agent.

Source: [Missing Semester: Course Overview and the Shell](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/course-shell/).
:::

## A command has a structure

| `git` | `log` | `--oneline` | `analysis.py` |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Program | Action | Option | Argument |

::: {.notes}
Arguments are strings supplied to a program. Options or flags modify the
program's behavior. The exact grammar differs across programs, so use
`<command> --help` or documentation when needed.

Students do not need to memorize every command. They need to read a command,
identify its parts, and verify its effect.

Source: [Missing Semester: Command-line Environment](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/command-line-environment/).
:::

## Location matters

```bash
$ pwd
/Users/you/research

$ ls
README.md  analysis.py  data  output

$ cd data
$ pwd
/Users/you/research/data
```

Most Git commands act on the repository that contains the current directory.

::: {.notes}
Define the current working directory. A relative path begins from this
directory. An absolute path begins from the root of the file system.

Many command-line mistakes are location mistakes. Before a consequential
command, students can use `pwd`, `ls`, and `git status` to verify context.
:::

## Prediction: where is the file?

```bash
$ pwd
/Users/you/research/code

$ ls ../data/raw
survey.csv

$ python clean.py ../data/raw/survey.csv
```

What path does `../data/raw/survey.csv` identify?

::: {.notes}
Ask students to interpret the path before revealing the answer. `..` means
the parent directory. From `research/code`, the path identifies
`research/data/raw/survey.csv`.

This question prepares students to understand why code that depends on an
unknown working directory is difficult to reproduce.
:::

## A small command-line vocabulary

| Goal | Command |
|---|---|
| Show the current directory | `pwd` |
| List files | `ls` |
| Change directory | `cd <path>` |
| Create a directory | `mkdir <path>` |
| Read a text file | `cat <file>` |
| Get help | `<command> --help` |

::: {.notes}
These examples use a Unix-style shell on macOS or Linux. Windows PowerShell
has related commands, but some syntax differs. Git concepts do not depend on
the shell.

Do not turn this section into a syntax survey. The core ideas are current
location, paths, programs, arguments, and observable output.
:::

## Prefer a recorded procedure

**Manual workflow**

> Open the CSV. Delete three rows. Rename two columns. Save a new file.

**Scripted workflow**

```bash
python code/clean.py data/raw/survey.csv data/derived/survey.csv
```

::: {.notes}
A script makes the transformation inspectable and repeatable. The command
records the program, input, and output. The script records the precise rules.

Manual review can remain part of research, but a manual data transformation
must be documented. Prefer scripts for transformations that a computer can
perform.
:::

## Git's data model {.section-divider}

## Git and GitHub are different

<div class="comparison">
<div>
<h3>Git</h3>
<p>Version-control software</p>
<p>Runs on your computer</p>
<p>Does not require the internet</p>
</div>
<div>
<h3>GitHub</h3>
<p>Hosts Git repositories</p>
<p>Supports sharing and review</p>
<p>Requires a network connection</p>
</div>
</div>

::: {.notes}
A local repository contains its own history. GitHub can store another copy of
that repository and provide web-based collaboration features.

Students will use GitHub in the course, but GitHub is not the version-control
system.
:::

## A Git repository contains a graph

<div class="commit-graph linear">
<div class="commit"><span>C1</span><small>Import data</small></div>
<div class="arrow">←</div>
<div class="commit"><span>C2</span><small>Clean data</small></div>
<div class="arrow">←</div>
<div class="commit current"><span>C3</span><small>Estimate model</small></div>
</div>

- Each commit records a snapshot
- Each commit identifies its parent
- The history records relationships, not only dates

::: {.notes}
The arrows point from a commit to its parent. Git history is a directed acyclic
graph. Students do not need that term, but they should understand that history
can branch and later merge.

The commit identifier is derived from content. Short labels such as C1 are for
teaching only; Git uses hashes.

Source: [Missing Semester: Version Control and Git](https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/version-control/).
:::

## A commit is more than a saved file

```text
commit 8e12c4a
Parent:  47d906b
Author:  Student Name
Date:    2026-09-16

    Correct treatment coding
```

A useful commit records one coherent change.

::: {.notes}
The snapshot covers the repository, not only one file. The parent connects the
snapshot to history. The message records intent.

Recommend small commits that leave the project in a coherent state. A commit
should be large enough to represent one meaningful change and small enough to
explain in one sentence.
:::

## Branches are movable labels

<div class="branch-graph">
<span class="graph-node">C1</span><span class="graph-arrow">←</span>
<span class="graph-node">C2</span><span class="graph-arrow">←</span>
<span class="graph-node">C3</span><span class="graph-arrow">←</span>
<span class="graph-node alt-node">C4</span>
<span class="graph-label main-label">main</span>
<span class="graph-label alt-label">alternative<br>(HEAD)</span>
</div>

`HEAD` identifies your current branch and commit.

::: {.notes}
A branch is not a second folder or a copy of every file. It is a movable name
that identifies one line of development. New commits advance the current
branch label.

HEAD records the current position. Keep the explanation at this level. The
students do not need Git's internal reference files.
:::

## Prediction: what moves?

```bash
git switch -c alternative-specification
# edit analysis.py
git add analysis.py
git commit -m "Estimate quadratic specification"
```

After the commit:

- Which branch label moves?
- Does `main` move?
- Which commit does `HEAD` identify?

::: {.notes}
Answer: `alternative-specification` moves to the new commit. `main` remains at
the prior commit. HEAD identifies the new commit through the current branch.

The value of the question is the prediction, not command memorization. Students
who can predict the graph can usually recover from an unfamiliar situation.
:::

## Three states before a commit

<div class="state-flow">
<div><strong>Working tree</strong><small>Files you edit</small></div>
<div class="flow-arrow">→<code>git add</code>→</div>
<div><strong>Staging area</strong><small>Proposed snapshot</small></div>
<div class="flow-arrow">→<code>git commit</code>→</div>
<div><strong>Repository</strong><small>Recorded snapshots</small></div>
</div>

::: {.notes}
The staging area is Git's proposed next snapshot. `git add` copies selected
file content into that proposal. It does not upload a file or permanently
record a commit.

The same file can have one recorded version, one staged version, and one newer
working-tree version at the same time.
:::

## Prediction: one file, three versions

```bash
# analysis.py contains model A
git add analysis.py

# analysis.py is edited and now contains model B
git commit -m "Estimate baseline model"
```

Which model does the commit contain?

::: {.notes}
The commit contains model A because that content was staged. Model B remains
in the working tree.

This is a productive surprise. It makes the staging area concrete and explains
why `git status` and both forms of `git diff` matter.
:::

## The core inspection loop

```bash
git status
git diff
git add analysis.py
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Estimate baseline model"
```

**Inspect before you change Git's state.**

::: {.notes}
`git status` summarizes the state. `git diff` shows unstaged changes.
`git diff --staged` shows the proposed commit. `git commit` records only the
staged content.

Students can ask an AI system for syntax. They must still inspect the files,
diff, and repository state before approving an action.
:::

## An individual research workflow {.section-divider}

## Start with a project directory

```text
wage-project/
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── code/
│   ├── clean.py
│   └── analyze.py
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── derived/
└── output/
```

```bash
cd wage-project
git init
```

::: {.notes}
Use this project for the remaining Git examples. `git init` creates a hidden
`.git` directory that stores objects and references. It does not place the
project on GitHub.

The exact directory names can vary. The important rule is to distinguish
source material, code, derived data, and output.
:::

## Inspect the initial state

```bash
$ git status --short
?? .gitignore
?? README.md
?? code/
```

`??` means that Git does not track the file.

::: {.notes}
Git does not automatically record every file inside the repository directory.
Untracked means that no commit contains the file and the file is not staged.

Use `git status` frequently. It is an observation command and is safe to run.
:::

## Select the first snapshot

```bash
git add README.md .gitignore code/
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Create analysis workflow"
```

The message completes the sentence: **This commit will...**

::: {.notes}
Do not recommend `git add .` as the only starting habit. Explicit paths make
the selection visible. `git add .` can be appropriate after the researcher
has inspected the complete status and ignore rules.

An imperative message such as “Create analysis workflow” states what the
commit does when applied.
:::

## Read the history

```bash
$ git log --oneline --decorate
3cb418f (HEAD -> main) Create analysis workflow
```

```bash
git show 3cb418f
git log --oneline -- code/analyze.py
```

History is useful only when commits and messages are informative.

::: {.notes}
`git show` displays a commit and its changes. Limiting `git log` to a file can
answer when and why that file changed.

The persistent log is one of Git's principal benefits for independent work.
It replaces memory and filename conventions with inspectable evidence.
:::

## Use a branch for an uncertain direction

```bash
git switch -c alternative-specification

# edit, run, and inspect the analysis

git add code/analyze.py
git commit -m "Estimate quadratic specification"
```

`main` still identifies the prior working version.

::: {.notes}
A branch is useful for work that might be kept, revised, or discarded. Examples
include an alternative specification, a large refactor, or a risky data change.

A quick local edit does not always need a branch. Use one when separation
reduces confusion or protects a stable line of work.
:::

## Compare before you decide

```bash
git diff main..alternative-specification
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate
```

Then choose:

- Keep developing the branch
- Merge the branch into `main`
- Leave the branch for later
- Delete the branch after rejecting the idea

::: {.notes}
The branch preserves both the code and the reasoning recorded in commits.
The researcher can compare specifications without maintaining parallel files.

If the work should become the main line, switch to `main` and merge the branch.
Show the command only if time permits. The mental model is the priority.
:::

## Returning to working code

```bash
git log --oneline
git show <commit>
```

First ask:

1. Are the changes committed?
2. Do I want to inspect, restore, or reverse them?
3. Has another person received the commits?

::: {.notes}
Do not teach one universal “undo” command. Recovery depends on the state and
the intended result.

Committed work is usually recoverable. Uncommitted discarded work may be lost.
Shared history requires extra care because rewriting it affects other copies.

For this lecture, demonstrate inspection of an earlier commit. Defer `reset`,
interactive rebase, and other history-editing commands. `git revert` is the
safer conceptual model for undoing a shared commit because it adds a new commit.
:::

## Prediction: what would you protect?

You have working code on `main`. You want to try a new estimator that may require many edits.

Before the experiment, what would you do?

1. Confirm that the working version is committed
2. Create a branch
3. Make and test the edits on that branch

::: {.notes}
Ask students for the steps before revealing them. The key protection is a
known committed state. The branch gives the experiment a separate name and
history.

An agent should receive the same instruction: verify a clean starting state,
create a named branch, make focused commits, and report the diff.
:::

## Keep unsuitable files out of Git

```text
# Private or restricted data
data/raw/

# Generated output
output/

# Local environments and system files
.venv/
.DS_Store
```

Commit `.gitignore` before Git tracks these files.

::: {.notes}
Do not commit secrets, restricted data, large raw datasets, local package
environments, or easily regenerated output. An ignore rule does not remove a
file that Git already tracks.

Generated output is a judgment call. A final paper or small reference result
may be useful to preserve. Large or frequently changing intermediate files
usually are not.
:::

## Remote repositories provide another copy

```bash
git clone <url>
git fetch
git push
```

- `clone`: create a local repository from a remote repository
- `fetch`: download remote commits and labels
- `push`: send local commits and update a remote label

::: {.notes}
Keep the remote model brief. A remote repository is another repository, not a
shared live folder. Git transfers commits and branch references between the
copies.

`git pull` combines fetch with integration. Separating the concepts prevents
students from treating pull as unexplained synchronization.
:::

## When you collaborate later

- Give each change a separate branch
- Make small, coherent commits
- Fetch before you integrate work
- Review the diff before you merge
- Use a pull request when review or discussion is useful

::: {.notes}
Pull requests are a hosting-platform workflow, not a core Git object. They are
useful when another person should inspect and discuss a proposed merge.

For this independent research course, students do not need to create pull
requests for routine work. The habits of focused branches, clear commits, and
diff review remain valuable.
:::

## Reproducible research {.section-divider}

## A Git repository is necessary, not sufficient

```text
Exact code       ✓
Input data       ?
Run order        ?
Package versions ?
Random seed      ?
System tools     ?
```

The commit identifies **what you wrote**, not every condition required to run it.

::: {.notes}
Use this checklist to reconnect the two parts of the lecture. Git identifies a
precise project state. Reproduction requires all material inputs and execution
conditions for that state.
:::

## Make the pipeline explicit

<div class="pipeline">
<div>Raw data</div><span>→</span><div>Cleaning script</div><span>→</span><div>Derived data</div><span>→</span><div>Analysis script</div><span>→</span><div>Tables and figures</div>
</div>

Each derived file should have a documented path back to its inputs and code.

::: {.notes}
The arrows represent executable transformations. A reader should not need to
infer an undocumented manual step between boxes.

Raw data are treated as inputs. Scripts create derived data and outputs. If
raw data cannot be shared, document how an authorized researcher can obtain
them and what files the scripts expect.
:::

## Record the computing environment

<div class="environment-stack">
<div><strong>Analysis</strong><span>Your scripts and notebooks</span></div>
<div><strong>Packages</strong><span>pandas &lt;version&gt;, numpy &lt;version&gt;, ...</span></div>
<div><strong>Language</strong><span>Python &lt;version&gt;</span></div>
<div><strong>System</strong><span>Operating system and external tools</span></div>
</div>

Different environments can produce different results.

::: {.notes}
A virtual environment isolates a project's packages from packages used by
other projects. A dependency file records which packages the project needs.
A lock file or other exact version record pins the resolved package versions.

Do not teach tool-specific setup here. The conceptual requirement is that a
future user can reconstruct the relevant environment. Exact needs depend on
the language, tools, and sensitivity of the analysis.
:::

## Isolation and pinning solve different problems

| Practice | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| Virtual environment | Which packages belong to this project? |
| Version pinning | Which package versions produced the result? |

```text
Project A → isolated environment → recorded versions
Project B → isolated environment → different recorded versions
```

::: {.notes}
An environment without recorded dependencies may work only on the researcher's
computer. A version list without isolation can conflict with packages from
other projects. Strong workflows use both concepts.

Version pinning improves repeatability but does not guarantee indefinite
reproduction. Systems, external services, and unavailable packages can still
change.
:::

## Control randomness

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1433)
sample = rng.choice(observations, size=500, replace=True)
```

- Set and record a seed
- Use the same random-number generator
- Document intentional variation across runs

::: {.notes}
A seed fixes the initial state of a pseudorandom number generator. The same
seed can reproduce a sequence when the generator and relevant software remain
the same.

A seed does not correct a flawed simulation or guarantee identical results
across all software and hardware. It removes one avoidable source of variation.
:::

## Use project-relative paths

```python
# Fragile: specific to one computer
data = read_csv("/Users/name/Desktop/project/data/survey.csv")

# Portable: relative to the project
data = read_csv("data/raw/survey.csv")
```

Do not make another user reproduce your personal directory structure.

::: {.notes}
The portable example still assumes a defined project root. The run instructions
must state where to execute the command, or the code should determine the root
reliably.

Also document file names, encodings, expected columns, and access restrictions
when these details affect the run.
:::

## The README is the entry point

A new reader should learn:

1. What the project does
2. Which data it requires
3. How to create the environment
4. Which command starts the workflow
5. Where the outputs appear

::: {.notes}
Test the README from a clean copy of the repository. Instructions that work only
because of unrecorded files or global packages are incomplete.

The README should link to more detailed documentation when necessary. Keep the
first successful run direct and visible.
:::

## Prediction: will this project reproduce?

```text
✓ Code is committed
✓ README says: "Run analysis.py"
✓ Random seed is set
✗ Raw data location is not documented
✗ Package versions are not recorded
✗ clean_final.csv was edited manually
```

What must change before another researcher can reproduce the result?

::: {.notes}
Ask students to identify each broken link. The project needs data-access and
file-location instructions, a recorded environment, and a scripted replacement
for the manual edit or an exact documented protocol.

The committed code and seed are useful but do not compensate for missing inputs
or an undocumented transformation.
:::

## Directing an AI agent {.agent-process}

Do not ask only: **“Fix my analysis.”**

Specify the process:

1. Inspect `README.md`, `git status`, and the recent history
2. Create a branch from the current clean commit
3. Change only the stated files
4. Run the documented checks
5. Show the diff and explain each commit

::: {.notes}
An agent can execute commands quickly. It cannot infer the researcher's
preferred repository state or acceptable evidence without instructions.

The Git mental model lets the researcher verify the agent's starting point,
scope, history, and proposed integration. The reproducibility model lets the
researcher require an executable and documented result.
:::

## One mental model

<div class="final-model">
<div><strong>Shell</strong><span>Express an action</span></div>
<div class="final-arrow">→</div>
<div><strong>Git</strong><span>Record project states</span></div>
<div class="final-arrow">→</div>
<div><strong>Reproducible project</strong><span>Reconstruct a result</span></div>
</div>

Organization is part of the research method.

::: {.notes}
Close by returning to the four opening questions: what changed, why it changed,
which version produced the result, and whether another person can produce it.

Git is not only a collaboration tool. For an independent researcher, it creates
an inspectable record of decisions and protects productive experimentation.
:::
